title: BepiColombo reaches its scheduled Mercury arrival day after eight years in space
subtitle: Space & Astronomy: Europe and Japan’s mission is preparing for a new view of the smallest planet’s giant core, shadowed ice deposits and magnetic environment. Orbital capture had not been confirmed in the official updates reviewed for this report.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: BepiColombo’s eight-year journey has reached the date set for one of its most consequential manoeuvres: capture into orbit around Mercury on 21 November. The European Space Agency’s published schedule places the two connected science orbiters at this milestone today, before they separate in December.

At this report’s 21 November cutoff, the official updates reviewed by ATHENA had not confirmed successful capture. A scheduled manoeuvre is not a completed one. The mission’s scientific promise can be explained now without presenting an anticipated arrival as an accomplished result.

The joint European–Japanese mission launched on 20 October 2018. ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter will investigate the surface and interior, while the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s Mio will examine the magnetic environment around the planet. NASA also contributes Strofio, an instrument designed to study Mercury’s extremely thin exosphere.
Arrival is a sequence, not a single finish line

ESA’s animation released on 19 November explains the planned capture: four thrusters on the European orbiter slow the connected spacecraft as it approaches Mercury’s south pole from the night side. The initial orbit is designed to be highly elongated, reaching approximately 590 kilometres above the surface at its closest point and 11,640 kilometres at its farthest.

That animation illustrates the intended manoeuvre; it is not footage proving that it happened. Following capture, ESA schedules the separation of Mio for 9–10 December. Further manoeuvres are intended to bring the European orbiter to its science orbit in March 2027, with science operations beginning in April.

One major step is already complete. The Mercury Transfer Module separated on 3 September, leaving the European orbiter responsible for the final approach with Mio still attached. ESA reports that a thruster test on 24 September delivered the first planned course correction in this configuration. Mission controllers also completed their final arrival-phase simulation on 29 October.

The distinction between arrival, separation and scientific operations matters. Getting into an initial orbit would be an engineering achievement, but it would not mean that every instrument had begun its full observing programme.
A small world with an outsized core

Mercury is the Solar System’s smallest planet, yet its metallic core extends to about 85 per cent of the planet’s radius, according to NASA. That figure describes radius, not the percentage of the planet’s volume. There is evidence that part of the core remains molten or liquid.

Understanding how such an interior developed is part of the larger scientific reason to return. Mercury provides a very different example of a rocky planet from Earth, and measurements of its surface, interior and surroundings can help test explanations of its history.

Its temperatures are equally striking. Sunlit ground can reach about 430°C, while nights can fall to approximately minus 180°C. Mercury has a thin exosphere rather than a substantial atmosphere that can retain and redistribute heat.

Yet intense sunshine does not reach everywhere. Deep polar craters contain permanently shadowed areas where ice can survive. NASA says its MESSENGER mission established that Mercury’s polar deposits are predominantly water ice. BepiColombo is therefore following substantial earlier evidence, not starting with an unsupported suggestion that a hot planet might conceal frozen water.

MESSENGER orbited Mercury from 2011 to 2015; Mariner 10 made earlier flybys in the 1970s. BepiColombo builds on those missions with two orbiters designed to make complementary observations. It would be the first mission to operate two spacecraft in Mercury orbit at the same time.

Mercury’s surface magnetic field is only about one per cent as strong as Earth’s, NASA says, but it interacts with the solar wind. Investigating that environment alongside the planet itself can connect processes that a photograph of a cratered surface cannot reveal.

For readers following the mission, the next meaningful announcement is explicit confirmation of capture, followed by the separate spacecraft deployments and instrument checks. The images accompanying this report are dated archive photographs, not pictures of today’s manoeuvre.

Eight years of international engineering have brought BepiColombo to a demanding threshold. The reward sought is more than an arrival image: it is a fuller explanation of how an unusually dense, fiercely heated and partly ice-bearing rocky world works.
